newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland guerrillas keep powder dry and hidden.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland guerrillas keep powder dry and hidden.

text.p: The most disputed pieces of Northern Ireleand's peace jigsaw are hidden in coal bunkers in working class Belfast or wrapped in plastic and buried beneath the green turf of picture postcard Ireland.
They are the guns, explosive and detonators the Irish Republican Army and its Protestant Loyalist rivals have ammassed in a 28-year conflict over the future of British rule in Northern Ireland.
Neither group will be expected to surrender immediately any of its weaponry when talks on a lasting settlement to one of the world's oldest guerrilla wars begins in earnest next September.

A special "Decommissioning Committee" set up to run alongside the political negotiations will have to oversee the guerrillas' surrender of a stock of weapons that only they know the size and location of.
Everything else is guesswork.
"Taking the guns out of Irish politics" is a slogan shared by the IRA and its Loyalist foes, the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), Ulster Freedom Fighters and Red Hand Commando.

Sunday's IRA truce will admit its political wing, Sinn Fein, to the talks, in the same way that an October 1994 truce by the Loyalists gained the small Ulster Democratic Party (UDP) and Progressive Unionist Party (PUP) to the negotiations last June.

But, security chiefs say, nothing will force the guerrillas to hand over their guns and there is no precedent in Ireland's bloody history for a peaceful arms surrender - ever. Some 3,200 have been killed in the latest violent campaign.
Any surrender of weapons will have to be voluntary and depend upon a political settlement which can be accepted by all sides, politicians in the negotiations say.

Even then, the history of guerrilla warfare in Northern Ireland is punctuated by splits and schisms and there are already breakaway groups on both sides of the sectarian divide which have not signed up for a ceasefire or the negotiations.

These include the Irish National Liberation Army (INLA), which split from the IRA in 1976 and whose masked men were out on the streets of Belfast this month during rioting over Protestant parades, firing salvoes at security patrols.
The INLA has deep marxist roots. Its membership is tiny but fanatic and believes that only force will drive Britain from its six-county province of Northern Ireland.

Its main claim to notoriety was the 1979 bombing of the car park of the British parliament which killed Airey Neave, a confidant of Margaret Thatcher. Only months later, Thatcher became British prime minister.

Then there is the shadowy Continuity Army Council (CAAC) which came to light last year when it bombed a hotel in Enniskillen last year. Little is known about its political hue, beyond its extremist nationalism.

Early this year a new Loyalist group exploded into the public consciousness, the Loyalist Volunteer Force, which broke from the UVF and UFF to continue what it says is a war to fight any moves to weaken Northern Ireland's British status.
It is thought to be the group that planted a series of bombs at Sinn Fein offices which failed to kill. But security forces fear that it is radical, committed and lethal.
Many politicians in Northern Ireland fear that weapons held by the IRA and main Loyalist extremist groups could be passed on to splinter factions if a settlement is not to their liking.
The amount of weaponry that could be passed on in this way is formidable and of sufficient sophistication and quantity to keep protagonists fighting well into the next century.
The IRA, security sources say, has the biggest stock of weaponry including up to three tonnes of the Czech-made semtex plastic explosive and hundreds of automatic weapons.

"In terms of assault rifles, for instance, the IRA has an over-supply and will not be obliged to import further large quantities for the forseeable future," the authoritative Jane's Defence review said recently.
The IRA also has machineguns, rocket-propelled grenades and at least one SAM-7 surface-to-air missile which it has never used, possibly because it is defective, it said.

Most of its weapons were smuggled in either from Libya, whose leader Colonel Muammar Gaddafi found an echo of his own "anti-imperialist struggle" in the IRA war two decades ago, or from republican sympathisers in the United States.
Much of this stock is hidden beneath bogs in rural southern Ireland and moved piece by piece for operations. The rest is hidden in private safe houses in Belfast and elsewhere.

Loyalists have also acquired commercial explosive in recent years but have bungled every single attack they have mounted since 1993, according to police, as well as a variety of automatic weapons bought on Europe's post cold-war black market.
